I believe taking breaks and exploring outside interests is essential for staying motivated and finding new perspectives in programming.

I'm a Computer Science major in my fourth year, and my schedule this semester is quite packed. I'm finally taking higher-level courses that I've been looking forward to. It's surreal to be at this stage, as it feels like just yesterday I was learning about simple data structures in an intro class. Now, I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even quantum computing basics. It's exciting to see how far I've come!
store.1: I'm a Computer Science major in my fourth year, and my schedule this semester is quite packed. I'm finally taking higher-level courses that I've been looking forward to. It's surreal to be at this stage, as it feels like just yesterday I was learning about simple data structures in an intro class. Now, I'm diving into complex algorithmic concepts, advanced system design, and even quantum computing basics. It's exciting to see how far I've come!
store.2: My favorite class this semester is definitely Advanced Algorithms. I'm fascinated by theory that directly connects to real-world problem-solving, such as optimizing pathfinding in large networks or finding the fastest way to handle huge datasets with minimal time complexity. We've been exploring dynamic programming approaches and approximation algorithms for NP-hard problems. It's mind-bending at times, but in a good, challenging way. Our professor is excellent; she has a talent for explaining complex concepts in an intuitive manner. She'll present a problem on the board that seems impossible to solve in polynomial time, and then she'll show us a strategy to approximate a solution. Every time I leave that class, my brain is buzzing.
store.3: Aside from Advanced Algorithms, my second-hardest class this semester is Distributed Systems(CS 2631). It's a lot of reading, group discussions, and we're working on a major project that simulates a decentralized file storage system. The group project is an adventure in itself. We have to collaborate with people who have different coding styles and sometimes different ideas about what the final product should look like. However, that's also its beauty. In a real-world setting, you're never working in a vacuum. You have to be able to integrate your code with others' and handle issues like concurrency and node failures. It can be nerve-wracking at times, like when I spent hours troubleshooting a weird bug that turned out to be a misplaced bracket in one of the config files. But once we fixed that and everything ran smoothly, it was a huge sense of accomplishment.
store.4: I'm also taking an elective in Game Design, which counts toward my major if I combine it with certain other classes. As a gamer at heart, this was a must-take. The professor is from the industry and worked on a couple of indie games that received decent traction. We're learning about basic 2D and 3D engines, implementing physics, and even a bit of user experience design. It's incredibly fun because every assignment is super creative. Last time, I had to design a mini-game based on a labyrinth concept, and it was all about balancing the difficulty curve so players wouldn't get frustrated and quit. Getting that design right was challenging, but it was also rewarding to see it come together.
store.5: I initially thought I might regret signing up for the Introduction to Quantum Computing class, but now I actually enjoy it. The professor's approach is to focus on conceptual understanding rather than pure math, which makes it more accessible. Of course, there is math involved, like linear algebra, but it's interspersed with code examples in frameworks that simulate quantum circuits. We're not actually building quantum computers, but we're modeling basic algorithms like Grover's and Shor's to see how they theoretically outperform classical methods. It's mind-blowing stuff that has made me rethink how I approach problems.
store.6: My Capstone Project course is the sink-or-swim part of senior year. We have the entire semester to conceptualize, design, and build a software solution that solves a real problem. My group and I decided to work on a project that uses machine learning to analyze social media sentiment for better emergency response. It involves reading a firehose of tweets or posts and analyzing them for words that might suggest a disaster or crisis. We're building an interface that city officials or campus security could use to see real-time alerts. This project is pulling together everything I've learned as a CS major, including database management, building an API, front-end interface, and the ML pipeline. We're also learning about project management and how to keep ourselves organized. One person on our team is the designated "Scrum Master," so each week we have sprints, daily stand-ups, and all that agile jazz. It's a lot, but if we can pull it off, I'll be super proud.
store.7: I'm also taking a humanities elective called Philosophy of Mind. It's my last required non-CS elective, and I chose it because it ties back into AI in interesting ways. We discuss consciousness, the concept of mind, and how it might apply to artificial intelligence. The class is smaller, so we have a lot of class discussions, which is a welcome change from all the coding in my other classes. It's nice to sit back and analyze abstract ideas sometimes. This class also helps me see the bigger picture, like the ethical implications of building AI systems that could one day mimic or simulate human thinking. Two weeks ago, I wrote a paper on whether strong AI could ever truly experience qualia, such as the subjective experience of color or pain. It's a huge topic in the philosophy world, and researching it was a fascinating experience. I believe bridging technical knowledge with ethical considerations is important, so I'm grateful for this perspective.
store.8: My schedule is quite packed, as you can imagine. Mondays and Wednesdays are the most hectic days. I start with Advanced Algorithms at 9:30 am, followed by a short break before my Distributed Systems lecture at 11:00 am. After lunch, I have the Capstone meeting, which can be a mix of lectures, lab work, and project team time. Tuesdays and Thursdays are a bit lighter with just Quantum Computing in the morning and Game Design in the afternoon. On Thursdays, I also have Philosophy of Mind in the evening, which can be tough if I'm tired from the rest of the day. Fridays are a bit more relaxed, with no scheduled classes, but I usually end up working on assignments, group projects, or labs. I also do some undergrad research hours in a lab focused on data visualization for big scientific data sets. It's interesting, but it definitely adds to the workload. I'm just trying to stay organized and make the most of this senior year.
store.9: The biggest challenge this semester is balancing the group projects. The Capstone project alone can consume around ten hours a week, and it's even more if we encounter a major bug or if the model isn't training properly. Additionally, the Distributed Systems project is another significant time-sink. My group tries to meet at least twice a week, and we also rely heavily on Slack or Discord to stay updated. Coordinating the schedules of five different people can be a mini-nightmare. However, despite the stress, it's also exciting. This is one of my last chances to fully invest in a project that's purely academic and focused on learning, without the pressures of an actual job environment.
store.10: Overall, I'm having a blast. I used to dread the tougher CS classes because I was worried I wouldn't keep up, but at this stage, I've gotten better at problem-solving and time management. I still pull the occasional late night, but it's never as scary as it once was. Being a senior has given me a sense of confidence; I know if I grind and keep my eye on the end goal, I'll eventually figure things out. The biggest takeaway is that after four years, you learn how to be resourceful, how to collaborate, and how to think critically. These classes are tough, no doubt, but they're also super rewarding. Everything I'm doing now feels like it's directly building toward my future career, and that's a pretty great feeling.
store.11: I'm a fourth-year computer science major with a passion for coding. My hobbies help me maintain a healthy balance between academics and personal interests. I believe taking breaks and exploring outside interests is essential for staying motivated and finding new perspectives in programming.
store.12: Sailing is a hobby that brings me a sense of freedom and challenge. It's a great way to clear my mind and exercise my problem-solving skills. I feel lucky to have grown up near a marina and to have the opportunity to continue sailing in college. It's a unique hobby that helps me stay grounded amidst the demands of academic life.
store.13: Regular gym workouts have become an essential part of my routine. It's a great way to balance out the sedentary nature of coding and improve my overall health. I enjoy tracking my progress and seeing the incremental improvements in my strength and energy levels. Exercise also helps me relieve stress and stay focused, which is crucial for managing a heavy course load. I'm glad I made the commitment to prioritize fitness in college.
store.14: Gaming is a hobby that allows me to relax and challenge myself in a different way. I enjoy co-op survival games for their problem-solving aspects and social elements. It's a great way to unwind and stay connected with friends. Additionally, I'm interested in game development and have dabbled in Unity and Unreal Engine. I hope to explore this further in the future, as it combines my passion for technology with creativity.
store.15: Reading has been a lifelong passion for me, thanks to my mom's love of literature. I enjoy getting lost in fantasy and sci-fi novels, and lately, I've been particularly interested in books that explore the intersection of artificial intelligence and humanity. Reading about AI-themed sci-fi helps me consider the ethical and social implications of the technology I'm studying. It's a great way to relax and also to explore philosophical questions about my future career.
store.16: I've found that scheduling my hobbies helps me maintain a healthy balance between academics and personal interests. By planning ahead, I can ensure that I have time for activities like sailing, gym workouts, gaming, and reading. It's all about finding the right mix and making the most of my free time. I believe this balance is crucial for my overall well-being and helps me stay motivated throughout the semester.
store.17: I enjoy combining my hobbies to create unique experiences. For example, I might spend the morning sailing on the lake, then switch to playing video games in the evening. I find that each hobby shares common qualities like teamwork, attention to detail, and problem-solving. It's fascinating to see how skills developed in one area can be applied to another. By combining my hobbies, I can explore different aspects of myself and have a more diverse and engaging life.
store.18: I believe that passion for hobbies is what allows me to find time for them, even with a busy schedule. By breaking down my hobbies into smaller increments, I can still enjoy them and maintain a healthy balance. Whether it's reading a chapter, sailing once a month, or playing a quick game, every bit counts. It's all about being intentional with my time and making the most of the moments I have available.
store.19: I'm glad I could share my passion for hobbies with you. It's wonderful to have a variety of interests that showcase different aspects of myself. From the calming world of reading to the thrill of sailing, the discipline of weightlifting to the excitement of co-op games, each hobby brings its own unique flavor to my life. It's great to have something beyond coding that I can share with others. Thank you for listening and being a part of my journey!
store.20: I've been involved in undergraduate research since the end of my sophomore year, and it's been an eye-opening experience. It's given me a glimpse into how knowledge is created in the tech world, and I'm glad to be a part of it. As a freshman, I didn't think research was something I'd be interested in. I was more into coding projects and hackathons. However, one of my professors noticed my ability to combine technical coding with user experience and suggested I apply for a research assistant position in a data visualization lab. I was initially hesitant due to the intimidation factor, but I decided to take the leap. It turned out to be a great decision.
